claims.claim: Arendt's tendency to abstract from inequality and hierarchy in The Human Condition stemmed from a premise that postwar emancipation, the welfare state, and capitalist abundance meant contemporary unfreedom was no longer about the unjust rule of some over others, but rather a relation of society as a whole to each member.
qualifications: referring specifically to Arendt's premise regarding the postwar world or her corner of it
claims.supporting_excerpt:
Rather, her tendency to abstract in this way was the upshot of a speci ﬁc and hugely problematic premise about the shape of the postwar world, or at least of Arendt ’s corner of it: that the political emancipa-
tion of the working class, the development of the welfare state, and the sheer
abundance of the postwar capitalist economy meant that the forms of unfree-
dom characteristic of the contemporary world no longer involved the unjust
rule of some over others, but, as it were, a relation of society as a whole to each
and all of its members.

claims.claim: Arendt used an undifferentiated first-person plural ('we') when writing about worrisome midcentury American societal tendencies, driven partly by a motivation to counteract the smugness of ascendant Cold War liberalism.
claims.supporting_excerpt:
this emphasis on what “we” are unthinkingly doing to
“ourselves” had some understandable, even admirable motivations: among
other things, it was meant to work against the smugness and self-congratula-
tion that too often characterized expressions of ascendant Cold War liberal-
ism.

must_not_be_lost: Complications to the sketch involving asymmetrical climate impacts, differing valences of indoor and outdoor spaces, and the limits of The Human Condition regarding global inequality and climate migration.
unresolved_context: Whether Hannah Arendt's framework in The Human Condition can adequately address the conflictual politics of climate change adaptations, global inequalities, and climate migration.
